hero.title: Inherit or compose?
intro.0: Can't we just inherit everything - even from three classes at once? It feels like the natural way to reuse code, and often it is. But it does not fit every case, and forcing it tends to make code harder to change later. Here you'll see when inheritance is the right tool, and the other way to build one thing out of smaller pieces - so you can pick the right one each time.
task.1.title: Inherit when it is truly is-a
task.1.context: Inheritance fits when the child genuinely is a kind of the parent. The `Animal` base is given. Write a `Dog` that inherits it (`: Animal`), so it gets `Breathe` for free, and add its own `Fetch()` that returns `"fetching"`.
task.1.goal.0: Write `Dog : Animal` with a `Fetch()` that returns `"fetching"`.
task.1.goal.1: Main breathes then fetches, so the output is two lines: breathing then fetching.
task.2.title: The is-a lie
task.2.context: Inheriting just to borrow a method is a lie: a parrot is not a kind of megaphone. The honest move is has-a - the parrot holds a megaphone. The `Megaphone` is given. Write a `Parrot` that is given a word in its constructor, holds a `Megaphone` as a part, and whose `Talk()` returns the megaphone's boosted word.
task.2.goal.0: Write a `Parrot` whose constructor takes a word, holds a `Megaphone` part, and `Talk()` returns the megaphone boosting that word.
task.2.goal.1: Main builds a parrot with hello, so the output is HELLO.
task.3.title: You cannot inherit three
task.3.context: A chimera needs wings, fins and paws - but C# allows only one base class, so `class Chimera : Wings, Fins, Paws` does not compile. Hold one of each as a part instead. The three part classes are given. Write `Chimera` holding all three, with a `Go()` that uses the wings to fly.
task.3.goal.0: Write a `Chimera` that holds a `Wings`, a `Fins` and a `Paws` part, with `Go()` returning the wings' `Fly()`.
task.3.goal.1: Main sends it off, so the output is flying.
task.4.title: Combine the parts
task.4.context: Holding the parts lets one creature do many things - by asking each part in turn. Write a `Chimera` whose `Show()` gathers a move from all three parts and joins them into one line.
task.4.goal.0: Write a `Chimera` (holding wings, fins and paws) with `Show()` returning `"flying, swimming, running"`.
task.5.title: Swap a part, leave the rest
task.5.context: A deep inheritance tree is rigid; parts are loose. The legs sit behind an `ILegs` promise, and `Chimera` is handed a pair through its constructor. The `DogLegs` is given. Write a `CheetahLegs` that keeps the `ILegs` promise and runs faster, and the creature swaps to it with no change to `Chimera`.
task.5.goal.1: Main hands the creature `CheetahLegs`, so the output is sprinting.
task.6.title: Inherit or compose? - recap
task.6.context: Inheritance has one honest use; for everything else, hold parts.
task.6.summaryIntro: Inheritance is for a true is-a relationship. To combine capabilities, hold parts - it stays flexible where a deep tree turns rigid.
task.6.summaryItems.0.title: is-a -
task.6.summaryItems.0.text: inherit only when the child really is a kind of the parent.
task.6.summaryItems.1.title: The is-a lie -
task.6.summaryItems.1.text: inheriting just to borrow a method misleads every reader.
task.6.summaryItems.2.title: has-a -
task.6.summaryItems.2.text: hold a part as a field and ask it to do the work.
task.6.summaryItems.3.title: One base class -
task.6.summaryItems.3.text: C# forbids inheriting three; compose the parts instead.
task.6.summaryItems.4.title: Swap a part -
task.6.summaryItems.4.text: behind an interface, replace one part without touching the rest.
concept.pr-single-inheritance.def: C# lets a class inherit from just one parent, so you combine several parts by holding them instead.
task.6.summaryItems.5.title: In SOLID -
task.6.summaryItems.5.text: "favour composition" is not a letter itself, but it keeps the **L** (Liskov) honest - no is-a lie - and makes the **O** (Open/Closed) swap easy.
